statements.impact_statement: The flaw lets an unprivileged user reach privileged mount operations through the setuid mount(8). The image removes every setuid and setgid bit, so mount runs with the rights of the caller, and /etc/fstab has no entries. The app runs as the unprivileged user app and never starts mount.

The flaw is in nsenter --join-cgroup run by a privileged operator. Nothing in the container runs nsenter: the only processes are gunicorn and its workers as the user app, and the app starts no other programs.
The flaw needs an fstab entry with X-mount.subdir that an unprivileged user may mount. /etc/fstab in the image has no entries, and mount has no setuid bit.
The flaw needs a restricted bind mount from fstab and the setuid mount(8). /etc/fstab in the image has no entries, and mount has no setuid bit.
The flaw needs a privileged program that calls the libacl path functions on a path an attacker controls. The app processes do not load libacl, and no process in the container runs as root.
The flaw is in the infocmp program, which is in ncurses-bin, not in these libraries or the terminal data.
The flaw is in the infocmp program. It is in the image, but nothing runs it: the app starts no other programs.
The flaw is in systemd-homed. These two packages contain only the libsystemd and libudev libraries; systemd-homed is not in the image.
The flaw is in the Perl module Archive::Tar. perl-base does not contain that module, and no other Perl modules are installed.

The flaw is in the FTS5 extension of SQLite. The library is in the image because liblastlog2-2 (util-linux, the last-login database) needs it, so removing it would break that package. The app talks to PostgreSQL, never imports sqlite3 and starts no program that loads either library: the security test checks that no process of the app has loaded libsqlite3 or liblastlog2 (MIT-41).

The flaw is in kadmind, the Kerberos administration server (or the RPC library it uses). Neither is in the image: it has only the four client libraries of krb5 (libgssapi-krb5-2, libk5crypto3, libkrb5-3, libkrb5support0), and no krb5-admin-server, libgssrpc4t64 or libkadm5srv-mit12 (SBoM).

The flaw is in the KDC, the Kerberos key distribution server (memory leak in the KDB keytab key code). Neither the KDC nor its database library is in the image: it has only the four client libraries of krb5 (SBoM).

The flaw is in the KDC, the Kerberos key distribution server (NULL dereference in the PKINIT pre-authentication; krb5-pkinit is not in the image either). Neither the KDC nor its database library is in the image: it has only the four client libraries of krb5 (SBoM).

The flaw is in the ASN.1 decoder that libkrb5 shares with the KDC (a read overrun that stops a KDC, according to the advisory title; the component is not described in the Debian tracker). An attacker reaches it with a message to or from a Kerberos server. The app talks to no Kerberos server: its database connection logs in with a password, not GSSAPI, there is no krb5.conf, no KRB5 variable and no ticket cache. The security test checks all four, in the running container (MIT-41).

The flaw is in decode_sequence_of(), in the ASN.1 decoder that libkrb5 shares with the KDC; an attacker reaches it with a request to a KDC, or, in a client, with a reply from a KDC they control. The app talks to no Kerberos server: its database connection logs in with a password, not GSSAPI, there is no krb5.conf, no KRB5 variable and no ticket cache. libpq loads libgssapi-krb5, but nothing in the app can send input to it. The security test checks all four, in the running container (MIT-41).

The flaw is in the handling of the CAMMAC authorization data (a container for authentication indicators); whether it sits in the KDC or in libkrb5 is not described in the Debian tracker. An attacker reaches it with a message to or from a Kerberos server. The app talks to no Kerberos server: its database connection logs in with a password, not GSSAPI, there is no krb5.conf, no KRB5 variable and no ticket cache. The security test checks all four, in the running container (MIT-41).

The flaw is in SQLite (FTS5 index). The library is in the image because liblastlog2-2 (util-linux, the last-login database) needs it, so removing it would break that package. The app talks to PostgreSQL, never imports sqlite3 and starts no program that loads either library: the security test checks that no process of the app has loaded libsqlite3 or liblastlog2 (MIT-41).
